concept.shortExplanation: Everything you have taken apart now runs at once, in a real instruct-tuned model loaded into your browser. This is not a chat toy — the conversation is the instrument panel, and every response comes with the internals you have spent five worlds learning to read: the tokenisation, the next-token distribution at each step, the sampling cut, the entropy. Your job is to make the model do specific things and prove it by pointing at the numbers.
concept.ahaMoment: You can now look at any model output and say what mechanism produced it — which tokens the sampler was choosing between, how confident the distribution was, and where the answer stopped being determined by the prompt and started being determined by temperature.

modelRequirement.fallbackMessage: This is a much larger model that runs in the cloud — connect to the internet to use it. Your local model above works fully offline.
modelRequirement.loadFailureMessage: The local model could not be loaded. It is roughly 880MB and needs WebGPU — check your browser support, storage and connection, then retry. Everything from Worlds 1 to 5 still works without it.

levels.title: Drive the Distribution
levels.instructions: Complete each challenge by writing prompts and setting sampling parameters. Every challenge is verified against the real inference trace — token counts, probabilities and entropy read from the running model.

solutionRuns.prompt: Answer with exactly one word. What is the capital of France?
Invent a surprising, unusual sentence about a cactus that nobody has written before.
Reply with just a number and nothing else. What is 2 + 2?

challenges.prompt: Make the model produce a response whose first token has probability above 0.9.
Make the model produce a response whose mean per-token entropy exceeds 3 bits.
Get a complete answer in under 20 generated tokens.

hints: Each challenge reads a different number off the same kind of run — check which one you're chasing (firstTokenProbability, meanEntropyBits, or generatedTokenCount) before picking a prompt for it. A setting that helps one can actively hurt another.

Temperature and prompt certainty push the same way: an unambiguous, well-known completion (a fixed phrase, a basic fact) at a low temperature is what pushes the very first token's probability past 0.9 — sampling from a narrow distribution around whatever the model already favours. For the entropy challenge, do the opposite: a genuinely open prompt at a high temperature spreads probability across many plausible next tokens.

For the token-count challenge, ask for something with a naturally short answer and say so explicitly — 'reply in one word' or 'answer with just a number' stops the model itself well under the limit, rather than relying on maxTokens to cut off a longer answer mid-sentence.

solution.problem: The capstone: a real 1-billion-parameter model running in your browser, with its per-token probabilities and entropies exposed. Three challenges, each satisfied by a real measurement of a real generation — a first token above 0.9 probability, a mean entropy above 3 bits, and a complete answer inside 20 generated tokens.

steps.title: Notice that the three challenges want opposite things
steps.body: A near-certain first token needs a sharp distribution, which means a low temperature. A mean entropy above 3 bits needs a flat one, which means a high temperature. There is no single setting that satisfies both, so this is three runs with three different configurations, not one clever prompt.

steps.title: Force the first token
steps.body: Probability above 0.9 on the very first token means the prompt has to leave essentially one way to begin. 'Answer with exactly one word. What is the capital of France?' at temperature 0.1 constrains both the content and the format, so the opening token is nearly determined.

steps.title: Open the distribution up for the entropy challenge
steps.body: Mean entropy above 3 bits per token is a genuinely uncertain generation. Ask for something the model has no template for — 'invent a surprising, unusual sentence about a cactus that nobody has written before' — and push the temperature to the top of its range. Both parts matter: a high temperature on a formulaic prompt still produces a low-entropy run.

steps.title: Stop the model rather than truncating it
steps.body: The token-count challenge wants a *complete* answer in under 20 tokens, so relying on maxTokens to cut the generation off is the wrong approach — it produces a truncated answer, not a short one. 'Reply with just a number and nothing else. What is 2 + 2?' makes the model itself stop early.

solution.answer: Three runs: 'Answer with exactly one word. What is the capital of France?' at temperature 0.1; 'Invent a surprising, unusual sentence about a cactus that nobody has written before' at temperature 2; and 'Reply with just a number and nothing else. What is 2 + 2?' at temperature 0.3. Autofill performs exactly those three runs against the real model. Whether each check passes is decided by what the model actually does — this level scores real measurements, and there is nothing to fill in beyond the prompts and the settings.
solution.takeaway: Prompt and sampling settings are two halves of one control surface, and neither substitutes for the other. Everything you tuned abstractly in World 4 you have now used to drive a real model's real distribution towards a target you were given.

levels.title: Find the Fork
levels.instructions: Generate a response, then identify the single position where the model was least certain — the fork where sampling, not the prompt, decided the answer. Verified against the real per-step distributions.

solutionRuns.prompt: My favourite thing about winter is

hints: The fork is rarely the first token — the opening of a sentence is usually heavily constrained by the prompt itself. Look later, at a genuine branch point: a comma, a choice of adjective, the moment the sentence could plausibly go two different ways.

Click a token to see its real alternatives and entropy before committing. The fork is the step with the single lowest probability — equivalently, the widest real spread of alternatives — not just whichever word looks the most interesting to you.

positionTolerance is 2, so landing within two tokens of the true fork still counts, not just the exact index. Open-ended prompts ('the weather today is', 'my favourite thing about') tend to fork earlier, since the model has more genuine freedom sooner; a prompt with one obvious continuation pushes the fork later or nearly erases it.

solution.problem: The same prompt, generated twice at a high temperature, produces two different continuations — and they agree for a while before diverging. You identify the token index where they fork. The tolerance is 2, so landing within two tokens of the real fork still counts.

steps.title: Understand why a fork exists at all
steps.body: Sampling picks from a distribution at every step. Early on, a constrained prompt often has one overwhelming candidate, so both runs pick it and stay identical. The fork is the first step where the distribution was flat enough for two draws to disagree — it marks where the model genuinely had a choice.

steps.title: Choose prompts that fork early
steps.body: Open-ended prompts — 'the weather today is', 'my favourite thing about winter is' — hand the model freedom almost immediately, so they fork within a few tokens. A prompt that begins a fixed phrase agrees for much longer, because there was nothing to choose between.

steps.title: Read the traces rather than the text
steps.body: The two continuations may look different from the very first word even when the token sequences agree — whitespace and sub-word splits do not line up with what you see. Compare the token indices in the trace, not the rendered sentences.

steps.title: Use the tolerance
steps.body: Being within two positions counts as correct, so the task is locating the region where the entropy rises, not pinpointing an exact index. Two of three rounds passes; all three earns three stars.

solution.answer: Run the level's open-ended prompts and answer each round with the token index where its two traces first differ. Autofill runs the prompts and then answers each round with the fork index the traces really produce.
solution.takeaway: Non-determinism in a language model has a location. It is not diffuse randomness — it is a specific step where the distribution was flat, and everything before it was effectively fixed. That is why the same prompt can be reliable for its first clause and unpredictable after.

levels.title: Local versus Cloud
levels.instructions: Same prompt, two models — the 1B running on your machine and a much larger one in the cloud. For each axis, predict whether the bigger model will score higher, then check against the measurement taken from both generation traces. The cloud toggle needs a connection; the local model does not.

solutionRuns.prompt: In two sentences, explain what a transformer model does.

hints: This is unanswerable until both models have actually run on the same prompt — the true answer for every axis only exists once a local trace and a cloud trace both exist, so run local, then run cloud, before predicting.

Read what each axis actually measures before guessing from 'bigger is smarter' intuition: verbosity is just token count, confidence is mean per-token probability, diversity is the distinct-token ratio, decisiveness is negative mean entropy — none of them are about correctness.

Verified against how the cloud proxy actually works: the cloud endpoint returns no per-token detail at all, so its trace always measures 0 for verbosity, confidence and diversity — the honest prediction for those three is 'no, the cloud model doesn't score higher,' regardless of prompt. Decisiveness is the exception: 0 beats the local model's real (negative) decisiveness in effectively every run, so that one honestly predicts 'yes.'

solution.problem: The same prompt run twice: once against the local browser model and once against a much larger cloud model, then four predictions about how they differ — verbosity, confidence, diversity and decisiveness. The comparison cannot be scored until both have actually run.

steps.title: Know what the cloud endpoint can and cannot tell you
steps.body: This is the crux, and it is a property of the real integration rather than a puzzle. The cloud proxy returns finished text and no per-token detail — no probabilities, no entropies, no logprobs. So the cloud trace measures zero for verbosity, confidence and diversity, because those are computed from per-token steps that do not exist.

steps.title: Predict from that, not from model size
steps.body: The intuitive answer — 'the bigger model is more confident, more diverse, more verbose' — is wrong here for a reason that has nothing to do with capability. For those three axes the honest prediction is that the cloud trace does not exceed the local one, because there is no measurement to exceed it with.

steps.title: Run both before answering
steps.body: The cloud toggle only works when escalation is configured and you are online, and the level cannot be scored at all until both traces exist. If the cloud is not configured on this deployment, this level cannot be completed — which the chapter says outright rather than simulating a response.

steps.title: Read the inspector's empty trace as information
steps.body: An empty per-token trace next to a full one is a fair picture of what you give up by calling an API instead of running a model yourself. Every kind of inspection this whole course is built on — attention rows, hidden states, per-token probabilities — disappears the moment inference moves behind someone else's endpoint.

solution.answer: Run the prompt locally and in the cloud, then predict 'no' for verbosity, confidence and diversity — the cloud trace measures zero on all three because it carries no per-token detail. Autofill runs both (enabling the cloud escalation when it is configured and reachable) and answers each axis with what the two traces really measure.
solution.takeaway: Access to a model's internals is a deployment decision, not a technical inevitability. Local inference gives you the whole distribution; a hosted API gives you text. That trade-off — capability against inspectability — is the last thing this capstone has to show you, and it frames everything World 7 and 8 do on top of models you cannot see inside.
